activity.title: This year has been a lot of changes. This summer, I’ve begun an internship as a Software Engineer Intern at Ironsite AI, working at a fast growing startup with engineers from Google Deepmind, Etched, Apple, and more, to build a product that’s for the boots, not the suits. It’s a mission I’m passionate about, and I can’t wait to be a part of it. I’m also in San Francisco, so I’m taking every opportunity I can get to venture into the startup world I can get. I already attended two hackathons in the last few days at WeaveHacks and Cursor x A16Z Night. I’ll be attending YC Startup School, YC’s internship fair, paper review nights, and nearly every luma event under the sun. The summer has just begun, but I’m ready to take it far. Every student at UMD uses AI. The question is whether they're learning anything from it. We built TerpTutor for the Cloudforce x Microsoft TerpAI track at Bitcamp 2026 — and it flips the script on how AI works in education. Most AI tools give students answers. TerpTutor is structurally incapable of doing that. It wraps UMD's TerpAI with Socratic prompting that forces students to think through problems step by step. But that's not the product. The product is what happens next. After every tutoring session, TerpTutor extracts a learning fingerprint — a structured map of what you know and what you don't. Then it finds another student whose strengths fill your gaps. It schedules your study session. And it moderates it by voice — two students sit together, say "Hey Terp," and an AI facilitator guides the conversation so you teach each other. The AI makes itself unnecessary. The more students teach peers, the less they need the AI. That's not a bug. That's the product. Built with TerpAI, Next.js, ElevenLabs, and the Web Speech API. 17 API endpoints. 6 phases. Zero databases. One hackathon weekend. #Bitcamp2026 #TerpAI #UMD #Hackathon #EdTech #AI ...more

Another weekend, another hackathon, and another win! This weekend at the UMD x Ironsite hackathon, my team and I tackled a problem different from most. Instead of working with clean, usable data, what if you had to solve spatial intelligence in the messy, real environment of a construction site? With Splatt, we did just that. Our team built a multimodal system that allows you to map out scenes in videos graphically in 2D and 3D, tracking camera paths, calculating object locations, and developing semantic vector databases on scenes for user queries. How, you might ask? By using the same tech as the Superman movies, constructing 4D models of scenes from 2D videos over time. Our technique, Gaussian Splatting, allows us to track information about camera paths using a model we optimize on every video run. We then used LangChain and multimodal Gemini-2.5-flash to feed in frames of these videos and collect descriptions and lists of objects with positions relative to the camera marked by timestamp in a Supabase vector database for rapid querying. We brought those results together, combining camera positions and object-to-camera positions to define global positions for every object and build our 4D Graph as well as our 2D Map representing the objects’ positions through time. In all, building Splatt was messy and rough, just like the scenes we had to reconstruct, but it’s because of the team I had and our willingness to brave through that that we made it out with our win. Thanks to Ian Coutinho , Mohammad Sadiq , @Vishal-Shah, and Aneesh Reddy for teaming up with me. This may be the Discrete Mathematicians’ first hackathon together, but it won’t be our last by a long shot, and we’ll be back at it again soon! If you want to check out our app, here are the links: Devpost: https://lnkd.in/eNbHFGfq GitHub: https://lnkd.in/egeagWcj App Demo: https://lnkd.in/emUJNRER #UMDxIronsite #AgenticAI #LangChain #GeminiAPI #SoftwareEngineering #3DGS ...more

What would you do if you were suddenly free of all work, expectations, exams, and quizzes? That was the question I faced nearly 40 days ago at the start of my Winter Break. While this past semester at UMD I’d been busy building AI agents and backend APIs, I wanted a project that was purely on my own to master Spring Boot and Docker. . Introducing CodeRunner, a full-stack platform for remote code execution. In this project, I dove straight into my work, mastering the Spring Boot Ecosystem, taking my java knowledge from GUIs in my CS classes to build robust MVC architecture with automated testing for a RESTful API. However, there were challenges I faced along the way: 1. Secure Sandboxing: To isolate untrusted code, I utilized Docker containerization, eventually implementing a Docker-in-Docker solution to both contain the Spring Boot API as well as manage execution environments. 2. Fault Tolerant Design: Transitioning from my native machine to a docker instance to a VM in Oracle Cloud, I needed a system that could handle failure. To accomplish this, I built a multi-threaded execution engine with process monitoring to prevent runaway processes and system deadlocks. 3. DevOps and Deployment: To deploy my app, I initially experimented with Railway and Fly.io , but a Docker-in-Docker solution didn’t mesh well with serverless platforms. Then, I found Oracle Cloud and Vercel. Deployment here was arduous. I spent days configuring VCN network groups, collecting SSL certificates, and connecting the frontend and backend, but seeing that first “Success” made all that effort all the more worth it. CodeRunner may end today as a personal project, but the skills it imprinted upon me, whether that’s container orchestration or real system design, are invaluable, and will never be forgotten. This is only one step in my journey, and I will take these tools with me into my upcoming semester at UMD. Check out the live frontend here: https://lnkd.in/eKu_A63w . #SoftwareEngineering #SpringBoot #Docker #CloudComputing #UMD #OracleCloud ...more

What a weekend at Hack@Brown. In my first formal hackathon, my team and I walked out with over $2,000, two track wins, and some incredible connections. We built RentSwarm, a multi-agent system that gives power back to renters. It uses five specialized agents to automate the housing search: 1. The Scout: Bypasses anti-bot filters with BrowserBase to filter Craigslist listings. 2. The Forecaster: Predicts ‘true cost of living’ beyond the sticker price on utilities, commute, and more. 3. The Negotiator: Uses RAG to cross-reference real negotiation tactics to get your best deal. 4. The Lawyer: Flags predatory lease policies by analyzing PDFs page-by-page via RAG. 5. The Chat: A centralized guide that synthesizes info from other agents. To make this more than a simple ‘Gemini Wrapper’, we used Next, TypeScript, LangChain, and LangGraph to create a multi-agent ecosystem. I focused on the cross-agent integration and cloud infrastructure, migrating our workflow to LangChain x Gemini, architecting a knowledge base with AWS Bedrock and S3 buckets, and containerizing the stack with Docker on AWS EC2. We went from nothing to a live, user-accessible domain in 24 hours. At the end, we took home the two awards: 1. Marshall Wace - Beyond the Prompt: Building Intelligent Generative Systems (1st, $2000) 2. MLH’s Best Use of Gemini API (Google Swag Kit) Huge thanks to Dylan G. and the Marshall Wace team for the insightful technical conversations and for sponsoring our track. Thanks to Hack@Brown and Major League Hacking for organizing the event, and most importantly, thanks to my incredible teammates Selin Ozsaracoglu , Maanya Chugh , and Olúwafẹràńmi Oyèlùdé for bringing the energy that got us our win. Since January of this past year, I've had the ambition to and the pleasure of starting up a robotics program in my town's local middle school. It began when a student approached me saying that there simply wasn't enough STEAM education at the middle school level in Glastonbury. The fact of the matter was, working with lego robots isn't enough for 7th & 8th graders. I knew something had to change, so I took matters into my own hands. With the help of Dana Kinel , as well as Jesse Wang , Sai Abishek Jeyackumar , Ilakkiya Tamilarasu , Aadhya Raj, and Garvit Singh, we brought the parts, designed the curriculum, and prepared engaging lessons every Monday for months of the school year. Students learned topics from Java fundamentals to OnShape basics, although we still found time to enjoy the yummy remnants of our monthly challenges. Then, this summer, I began an unofficial FIRST Tech Challenge team in the middle school. This team, while not having the funds to compete yet, has learned Java & build techniques under my guidance, as well as the guidance of my fellow student volunteers. Over this time, I taught twice a week for two hours each, but I also aimed to push the students to have their own mobility in solving problems. Of course, all good things come to an end, so now that I'm heading off to UMD, I'm leaving this program in very capable hands. In all, I got to work with an incredible group of students, and I look forward to seeing what success this program has beyond my departure from Glastonbury. Go Galactic Guardians! ...more

Somewhere in the USA 3 AM wake-up is a habit, 4 AM start time is a standard, and a 12-hour work day is required. A foreman reminds his crew to stay focused, then grins and tells them, "let's get hot." Somewhere in the USA, a superintendent echoes, “you are your brothers’ and sisters’ keeper. Safety got us here, and looking out for one another gets us home.” Somewhere in the USA, the energy we consume is searched for and found, in the oil and wind fields of west Texas. The stadiums we gather in and the schools we learn in are built. Traveling from the dazzling skyline of San Francisco, to the sprawling plains of Abilene, the lush greenery of Appalachia, and into the heart of DC, all in a week's time. It changes your perspective on what it means to be a builder in this country. I've seen the common thread from site to site, crew to crew: pride, grit, purpose. Somewhere in the USA, the world around us is being built, whether right in front of our very eyes or 3,000 miles away, by early mornings, by making the impossible possible, by people, on a team, showing up to do their part. Getting to witness this firsthand is an honor. And we haven't scratched the surface yet. Somewhere new in the USA, I'll be tomorrow. And the next day. And every day after.

Construction doesn’t have a labor problem. It has a black box problem. The first project I ran on my own, my boss handed me a budget and said, “This budget is your box. Live inside it. Plan the work, work the plan.” Then he gave me a stack of spreadsheets and wished me luck. The budget was never the problem. The problem was that the spreadsheets assumed the job would go exactly as planned. They didn’t account for the excavation delays and compressed anchor bolt install, the design info that showed up late, or the underground fire water tank that became a five-month out-of-sequence delay. The production reports told me weekly where I was. They never told me why I got there. That’s the black box of construction: everything that happens between production reports. It’s the gap between what happened and why it happened. The decisions, constraints, delays, and coordination challenges that no spreadsheet captures. Without visibility into that work, uncertainty compounds week over week until we get to the end of the job asking, How did we get here? or How are we going to finish strong? It sits between the estimate and the final cost, yesterday’s production and today’s, hours worked and work actually installed. Inside it are the decisions, delays, rework, and coordination failures that decide whether a crew succeeds or struggles. Yet we still try to run operations with accounting tools: hours in, quantities out. Then we wonder why productivity is so hard to improve. Last week our team was at the CII Elevate Summit in Denver. What stuck with me was a question that kept coming up: do we actually understand how work happens on site, not just what it costs? Because once you understand the why, everything downstream gets better: estimating, scheduling, forecasting, and the daily calls superintendents have to make. And crews spend less time fighting problems they didn’t create. Construction has never lacked hardworking people. We’ve always had exceptional builders. What we’ve lacked is visibility into the black box between planning and production. It’s time we stopped asking our people to outperform with bad information and started giving them better information instead. (That water tank taught me a lot about not giving up, I’ve been using that skill a lot these days)
